stem: (Supplement) In which organ is urea made?

options.content: Liver
options.rationale: The liver makes urea from excess amino acids.

options.content: Kidney
options.rationale: The kidneys remove urea from the blood; they do not make it.

options.content: Bladder
options.rationale: The bladder stores urine.

options.content: Lungs
options.rationale: The lungs excrete carbon dioxide.

explanation: Urea is made in the liver when excess amino acids are broken down (deaminated). The blood carries it to the kidneys, which excrete it in urine.
hints: Which organ deals with excess amino acids?

stem: Which tube carries urine from a kidney to the bladder?

options.content: Urethra
options.rationale: The urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body.

options.content: Renal vein
options.rationale: The renal vein carries blood, not urine.

options.content: Ureter
options.rationale: Each kidney has a ureter leading to the bladder.

options.content: Renal artery
options.rationale: The renal artery brings blood to the kidney.

explanation: Urine leaves each kidney through a ureter and is stored in the bladder. It leaves the body through the urethra.
hints: There are two of these tubes, one from each kidney.

stem: True or false: urea is made in the kidneys.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Urea is made in the liver; the kidneys remove it from the blood.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. The liver makes urea from excess amino acids; the kidneys excrete it.

explanation: The liver makes urea when it breaks down excess amino acids. The blood carries the urea to the kidneys, which filter it out and excrete it in urine.
hints: Which organ breaks down excess amino acids?

stem: Which excretory product is removed from the body by the lungs?

options.content: Urea
options.rationale: Urea is excreted by the kidneys in urine.

options.content: Oxygen
options.rationale: Oxygen is taken in; it is not a waste product.

options.content: Undigested fibre
options.rationale: Undigested food is egested as faeces.

options.content: Carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is a waste product of respiration, breathed out.

explanation: Carbon dioxide, a waste product of respiration in cells, diffuses into the alveoli and is breathed out. The kidneys excrete urea, excess water and excess ions.
hints: Which waste product of respiration is a gas?

stem: Name the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body.

rejected.feedback: Ureters carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

explanation: The urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body. Do not confuse it with the ureters, which carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.
hints: It is not the ureter.

stem: Match each part of the urinary system with its function.

right.content: Filters the blood and makes urine
Carries urine from a kidney to the bladder
Carries urine out of the body

explanation: The kidneys filter blood and make urine; the ureters carry it to the bladder, which stores it; the urethra carries it out. The renal artery (not listed) carries blood to the kidney.
hints: One function belongs to a blood vessel.

stem: Which statement describes **excretion**?

options.content: Passing out undigested food as faeces
options.rationale: That is egestion.

options.content: Removing waste products of metabolism, toxic substances and substances in excess
options.rationale: For example, carbon dioxide and urea.

options.content: Taking food into the body through the mouth
options.rationale: That is ingestion.

options.content: Releasing digestive enzymes into the gut
options.rationale: That is secretion.

explanation: Excretion removes waste products of the chemical reactions in cells (such as carbon dioxide and urea), toxic substances and substances in excess (such as extra water and ions).
hints: Excreted substances have been made by, or been inside, the body's cells.

stem: (Supplement) Which substances are filtered out of the blood into the capsule around the glomerulus?

options.content: Water, glucose, red blood cells and proteins
options.rationale: Red blood cells and proteins are too large to be filtered.

options.content: Urea only
options.rationale: Many small molecules are filtered, not just urea.

options.content: Water, glucose, urea and mineral ions
options.rationale: Small molecules and ions are forced out by the high pressure.

options.content: Proteins and platelets
options.rationale: These are too large and stay in the blood.

explanation: In the glomerulus, blood at high pressure forces water and small dissolved molecules and ions (glucose, urea, mineral ions) into the capsule. Blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.
hints: Which of these are small enough to pass through the filter?

stem: (Supplement) As the filtrate passes along the tubule of a nephron, which substances are reabsorbed into the blood?

options.content: All of the glucose, some of the ions and most of the water
options.rationale: This is what the nephron reabsorbs.

options.content: All of the urea, all of the water and all of the ions
options.rationale: Urea is not reabsorbed in this way; most of it stays in the urine.

options.content: Some of the glucose and all of the urea
options.rationale: All the glucose is reabsorbed, and much of the urea stays in the filtrate and leaves in the urine.

options.content: Only the proteins
options.rationale: Proteins are not filtered in the first place.

explanation: The nephron reabsorbs all the glucose, some of the ions and most of the water back into the blood. Urea, excess water and excess ions remain and form urine.
hints: Which useful sugar should never be lost in urine?

stem: (Supplement) What is **deamination**?

options.content: The building of amino acids into proteins
options.rationale: That is assimilation (protein synthesis).

options.content: The digestion of proteins into amino acids
options.rationale: That is done by proteases.

options.content: The filtering of urea out of the blood
options.rationale: That happens in the kidneys.

options.content: The removal of the nitrogen-containing part of excess amino acids in the liver, forming urea
options.rationale: The rest of the molecule can be respired or stored.

explanation: In deamination, the liver removes the nitrogen-containing part of excess amino acids. This nitrogen is turned into urea, which is excreted by the kidneys.
hints: The 'amine' part of an amino acid contains nitrogen.

stem: (Supplement) Why must urea be excreted?

options.content: It is needed by the kidneys as a source of energy.
options.rationale: Urea is a waste, not a fuel.

options.content: It is toxic, so it would damage cells if it built up in the body.
options.rationale: Urea must be kept at a low concentration in the blood.

options.content: It makes the blood too thick to flow.
options.rationale: Urea is dissolved in the plasma; toxicity is the problem.

options.content: It is a source of protein the body cannot use.
options.rationale: Urea is not a protein.

explanation: Urea is toxic. If it were not excreted, its concentration in the blood would rise and it would damage cells, so the kidneys remove it in urine.
hints: What would happen if urea kept building up in the blood?

stem: (Supplement) Complete the sentences about the nephron.

payload.template: Blood is filtered at high pressure in the {{blank:glo}}. As the filtrate flows along the tubule, all of the {{blank:glu}} is reabsorbed into the blood. Urine contains urea, excess water and excess {{blank:ions}}.

explanation: Filtration happens in the glomerulus. All the glucose, some ions and most of the water are reabsorbed. Urine contains urea, excess water and excess ions.
hints: The filter is a knot of capillaries.

stem: (Supplement) In one day a person's kidneys produced 170 dm³ of filtrate and 1.7 dm³ of urine. Calculate the percentage of the filtrate that was reabsorbed.
explanation: Reabsorbed $= 170 - 1.7 = 168.3\ \text{dm}^3$. Percentage $= \dfrac{168.3}{170} \times 100 = 99.0\%$.
hints: Find the volume that did not end up in the urine.

stem: (Supplement) The concentration of urea is 0.25 g per dm³ in a person's blood plasma and 18 g per dm³ in their urine. How many times more concentrated is the urea in the urine?
explanation: $\dfrac{18}{0.25} = 72$, so urea is 72 times more concentrated in urine than in plasma, because most of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed.
hints: Divide the concentration in urine by the concentration in plasma.

stem: Farai works outdoors in Kariba on a very hot day and sweats a lot, but drinks little. How will his urine change?

options.content: A large volume of dilute urine
options.rationale: That happens after drinking a lot of water.

options.content: No change, because sweat and urine are not linked
options.rationale: Losing water in sweat makes the kidneys save water.

options.content: A small volume of concentrated, dark urine
options.rationale: The kidneys reabsorb more water to keep the blood's water content constant.

options.content: Urine containing glucose
options.rationale: Glucose in urine is a sign of diabetes, not of sweating.

explanation: Sweating removes water from the blood. The kidneys respond by reabsorbing more water (osmoregulation), so he produces a small volume of concentrated, dark urine.
hints: The kidneys try to keep the water content of the blood constant.

stem: Which substances are excreted by the skin in sweat?

options.content: Water, salts and a small amount of urea
options.rationale: Sweat glands remove these, though sweating is mainly for cooling.

options.content: Carbon dioxide and oxygen
options.rationale: These gases are exchanged in the lungs.

options.content: Glucose and amino acids
options.rationale: These useful substances are not excreted.

options.content: Bile and faeces
options.rationale: These leave through the gut.

explanation: Sweat contains water, salts and a little urea, so the skin is an excretory organ, although the main role of sweating is to cool the body.
hints: Why does sweat taste salty?

stem: What should the dialysis fluid used in a kidney machine contain?

options.content: Urea at a high concentration, to push it into the blood
options.rationale: Urea is meant to leave the blood.

options.content: No glucose and no ions
options.rationale: Glucose and ions would then diffuse out of the blood, which would be harmful.

options.content: Red blood cells, to replace those lost
options.rationale: Blood cells cannot cross the membrane, and none are lost.

options.content: Glucose and ions at the normal blood concentrations, but no urea
options.rationale: Urea diffuses out; glucose and normal ion levels stay in the blood.

explanation: With no urea in the fluid, urea diffuses out of the blood down its concentration gradient. Glucose and ions are at the normal blood concentrations, so the patient keeps the glucose, while any excess ions diffuse out.
hints: Which substances should leave the blood, and which should stay?

stem:
(Supplement) The table shows the concentrations of some substances in the blood plasma, the filtrate and the urine of a healthy person.

| Substance | Plasma / g per dm³ | Filtrate / g per dm³ | Urine / g per dm³ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Glucose | 0.9 | 0.9 | 0 |
| Protein | 75 | 0 | 0 |
| Urea | 0.28 | 0.28 | 19.6 |
| Sodium ions | 3.3 | 3.3 | 5.0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Why is there no protein in the filtrate?

options.content: All the protein is reabsorbed in the tubule.
options.rationale: Protein never gets into the filtrate in the first place.

options.content: Protein molecules are too large to be filtered out of the glomerulus.
options.rationale: Only small molecules and ions pass into the capsule.

options.content: The liver turns all the protein into urea first.
options.rationale: Plasma proteins remain in the blood.

options.content: Protein is used up as fuel by the kidney.
options.rationale: This is not why it is absent from the filtrate.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why glucose is present in the filtrate but not in the urine.

points.description: Glucose molecules are small enough to be filtered (same concentration in plasma and filtrate)
All the glucose is reabsorbed into the blood as the filtrate flows along the tubule

parts.explanation: Glucose is small enough to be filtered, so it has the same concentration in plasma and filtrate, but all of it is reabsorbed into the blood from the tubule, so none reaches the urine.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in the urine than in the filtrate.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the concentration of urea increases between the filtrate and the urine.

points.description: Most of the water is reabsorbed (while most urea is not), so the urea becomes more concentrated

parts.explanation: Most of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed but most of the urea is not, so the urea is left in a much smaller volume and becomes more concentrated.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: A test shows glucose in another person's urine. Suggest what this might indicate.

points.description: Diabetes / blood glucose concentration too high, so not all the glucose can be reabsorbed

parts.explanation: It suggests diabetes: the blood glucose concentration is so high that the tubules cannot reabsorb all of it.

explanation: Protein is too large to be filtered. Glucose is filtered and then all reabsorbed. Urea is concentrated $\dfrac{19.6}{0.28} = 70$ times because most of the water is reabsorbed. Glucose in urine suggests diabetes.
hints: Compare plasma with filtrate (filtration), then filtrate with urine (reabsorption).

stem: Mrs Ncube's kidneys have failed and she has dialysis three times a week. The urea concentration of her blood was 1.8 g per dm³ at the start of a session and 0.45 g per dm³ at the end.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage decrease in the urea concentration of her blood during the session.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how urea leaves her blood in the dialysis machine.

points.description: Urea diffuses through the partially permeable membrane / dialysis tubing
from the blood (high concentration) into the dialysis fluid, which contains no urea (low concentration)

parts.explanation: Urea diffuses through the partially permeable membrane from her blood, where its concentration is high, into the dialysis fluid, which contains no urea.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why she does not lose glucose from her blood during dialysis.

points.description: The dialysis fluid contains glucose at the same concentration as normal blood, so there is no concentration gradient / no net diffusion

parts.explanation: The dialysis fluid contains glucose at the same concentration as normal blood, so there is no concentration gradient and no net diffusion of glucose.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why fresh dialysis fluid flows continuously through the machine.

points.description: To keep the urea concentration in the fluid low, maintaining a steep concentration gradient (so urea keeps diffusing out)

parts.explanation: Fresh fluid keeps the urea concentration in the fluid low, so the concentration gradient stays steep and urea keeps diffusing out of the blood.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the proteins in her blood are not lost into the fluid.

points.description: Protein molecules are too large to pass through the membrane

parts.explanation: Protein molecules are too large to pass through the pores of the partially permeable membrane.

explanation: Decrease $= 1.8 - 0.45 = 1.35$ g per dm³, which is $\dfrac{1.35}{1.8} \times 100 = 75\%$. Urea diffuses into fluid that contains none; glucose stays because the fluid matches normal blood; fresh fluid keeps the gradient steep; proteins are too large to cross the membrane.
hints: Explain every movement using diffusion and concentration gradients.

stem: (Supplement) Describe the role of the liver in the formation of urea, and explain why urea must be removed from the body. [5]

points.description: Amino acids from digestion are carried to the liver (in the hepatic portal vein)
Some are assimilated into proteins (e.g. plasma proteins)
Excess amino acids cannot be stored
They are deaminated: the nitrogen-containing part is removed
and converted into urea, which passes into the blood and is carried to the kidneys
Urea is toxic / would damage cells if it built up, so it must be excreted

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Amino acids absorbed from the small intestine are carried to the liver in the hepatic portal vein. The liver uses some of them to make proteins, such as plasma proteins. Excess amino acids cannot be stored, so the liver deaminates them: it removes the nitrogen-containing part of each molecule and converts it into urea, while the rest of the molecule can be respired. The urea passes into the blood plasma and is carried to the kidneys, which excrete it in urine. Urea must be removed because it is toxic: if it built up in the blood it would damage the body's cells.

explanation: The liver deaminates excess amino acids, forming urea, which is toxic and must be excreted by the kidneys.
hints: What happens to amino acids the body does not need?

stem: (Supplement) Explain how a nephron produces urine from the blood that enters the kidney. [6]

points.description: Blood arrives in the renal artery and enters the glomerulus at high pressure
Water, glucose, urea and ions are filtered into the capsule (filtrate)
Blood cells and large proteins are too big and stay in the blood
All the glucose is reabsorbed into the blood from the tubule
Some ions and most of the water are reabsorbed
The remaining liquid (urea, excess water, excess ions) is urine, which passes to the collecting duct / pelvis / ureter

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Blood containing urea enters the kidney in the renal artery and passes into a glomerulus, a knot of capillaries, at high pressure. The pressure forces water, glucose, urea and mineral ions out of the blood into the capsule surrounding the glomerulus, forming the filtrate; blood cells and large proteins are too big to pass through and stay in the blood. As the filtrate flows along the tubule, all of the glucose, some of the ions and most of the water are reabsorbed into the capillaries around the tubule. The liquid that remains, containing urea, excess water and excess ions, is urine. It flows into a collecting duct and then to the pelvis and the ureter.

explanation: Urine forms by filtration in the glomerulus followed by reabsorption of all the glucose, some ions and most of the water in the tubule.
hints: Describe filtration first, then reabsorption.
Say which substances are filtered and which are reabsorbed.

stem: Which substance is **not** normally found in the urine of a healthy person?

options.content: Urea
options.rationale: Urea is the main waste in urine.

options.content: Glucose
options.rationale: All the filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed.

options.content: Water
options.rationale: Urine is mostly water.

options.content: Salts (ions)
options.rationale: Excess ions are excreted in urine.

explanation: In a healthy person all the glucose that is filtered is reabsorbed, so urine contains urea, water and excess ions but no glucose. Glucose in urine is a sign of diabetes.
hints: Which useful substance is always reabsorbed?

stem: True or false: urine collects in the pelvis of the kidney before it passes into the ureter.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. The pelvis is the funnel-shaped space where urine from the collecting ducts gathers.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Urine drains from the collecting ducts into the pelvis and then into the ureter.

explanation: The kidney has an outer cortex, an inner medulla and a pelvis. Urine from the collecting ducts drains into the pelvis and then into the ureter.
hints: The pelvis is the funnel-shaped space at the centre of the kidney.

stem:
At the start of an investigation (0 minutes), a student drank 1 dm³ of water. Her urine was collected every 30 minutes.

| Time period / min | 0–30 | 30–60 | 60–90 | 90–120 | 120–150 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Volume of urine / cm³ | 120 | 310 | 260 | 90 | 40 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total volume of urine she produced in the 150 minutes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: In which period did she produce urine fastest?

options.content: 0–30 minutes
options.rationale: Only 120 cm³ was produced in this period.

options.content: 30–60 minutes
options.rationale: 310 cm³, the largest volume in any 30 minutes.

options.content: 60–90 minutes
options.rationale: 260 cm³ is less than in the period before.

options.content: 120–150 minutes
options.rationale: Only 40 cm³ was produced.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain the changes in urine production after she drank the water.

points.description: The water was absorbed into the blood, so the water content of the blood rose
This was detected (by the brain) and the kidneys reabsorbed less water
so a large volume of urine was produced (osmoregulation)
Once the extra water had been removed, the volume of urine fell back to normal

parts.explanation: The water was absorbed into her blood, raising its water content. This was detected by the brain, less ADH was released and her kidneys reabsorbed less water, so she produced a large volume of urine, peaking in the 30–60 minute period. Once the extra water had been removed, the volume fell back to normal: osmoregulation.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Predict the appearance of the urine she produced between 30 and 60 minutes.

points.description: Pale / dilute (low concentration of urea and salts)

parts.explanation: It would be pale and dilute, because a lot of water was being excreted with the same amount of urea and salts.

explanation: Total $= 120 + 310 + 260 + 90 + 40 = 820\ \text{cm}^3$. The kidneys removed the extra water by reabsorbing less, producing a large volume of dilute urine that peaked 30–60 minutes after drinking, then returned to normal: osmoregulation keeps the water content of the blood constant.
hints: Add the volumes for all five periods.
What do the kidneys do when the blood contains extra water?
